title: Tales of Genetics: Lifting Anomalies
summary: He contrasts two gym regulars: a genetically gifted former swimmer who trained stupidly on cables, never progressed and got fat, and a short lifter with nerve damage who stayed positive and slowly built a decent upper body. Attitude and behavior matter more than the cards you are dealt.
claims: Truly cursed lifters exist but are rare; most people who think they are hardgainers are actually just lazy
Putting in many hours means nothing if what you do in the gym is bogus
The gifted guy (6 ft former swimmer) refused barbells and dumbbells, only did cable circuits and one-rep maxes on full cable stacks, yet had a back like a smaller Ronnie Coleman from pure genetics

The cursed guy (about 5'6, bottom heavy) had nerve damage limiting upper body growth: after years he could barely curl 25 lb, stalled near 120 lb on bench, 135 lb was an accomplishment, though his legs were strong
The cursed guy was so dedicated he kept a second gym membership near his job to do accessory work at lunch
Despite his handicap, the cursed guy never complained, never missed a day, stayed cheerful, and after years began to look jacked in the upper body
The gifted guy never progressed in two years, got fatter and fatter and finally quit, burying his potential under fat
Genetics matter less than how you play your cards; with the right spirit you can beat people with better hands
If you get muscle cramps so bad at night you cannot sleep, question your training rather than continuing to max out daily
Gifted people often credit their results to hard work, never review their methods, then blame genetics when they fall off
The gifted guy was disliked and the other loved: how people treat you depends on your behavior; you cannot choose to be gifted but you can choose how you behave
